paper.title: Location-specific wage effects from offshoring and backshoring
paper.code_data_availability: Data Availability Statement (p. 11): “The register panel data used for individuals in dependent work and firms is sensitive data and is available through and under conditions of the researcher scheme of Statistics Denmark. …

registers.name_in_paper: Danish linked employer-employee register panel data (employee-employer linked register panel data covering all Danish employees)
Employer information linked to employee data (firm size, location and other firm demographics)
Firm internationalization questionnaire data (VOUT) – Danish International organization and outsourcing statistics, Statistics Denmark surveys of 2007, 2011 and 2016
registers.years: survey waves 2007, 2011, 2016 covering GVC activity in 2001-2006, 2009-2011 and 2014-2016
variables_mentioned: Have you backshored previously offshored business functions?
What business functions were offshored or backshored?
What was the destination country of your offshoring activity?

registers.name_in_paper: Eurostat, Entreprises sourcing abroad, variable egi_so1
registers.role: stylized facts (Fig. 1), not used in estimation

linkages: Firm internationalization questionnaire data (VOUT) matched to employed register data from Statistics Denmark
Employee data are linked to employer information on firm size, location and other firm demographics
Firms are located in 98 Danish municipalities (LAU level 2), classified into urban (“city” and “middle/urban”) and rural (“rural” and “periphery”) following Kristensen et al. (2006)
Workers are linked to the firm-level treatment dummies, which vary unisono for all persons employed in the firm

sample.universe: All Danish employees 2001-2016 in private firms located in Denmark with at least 20 employees that are covered by the Statistics Denmark VOUT firm surveys (population data for firms with 50+ employees; voluntary participation for firms with 20-49 employees in manufacturing NACE 15-37 and business services NACE 72-74)
sample.unit_of_observation: person-year (worker k employed in firm m located in municipality i in year t)
selection_rules: Population data for all private firms located in Denmark with 50 or more employees; firms with 20-49 employees in manufacturing (NACE: 15-37) and business services (NACE: 72-74) were given the opportunity of voluntary participation in the survey
When matching the linked employer-employee data with the firm surveys on GVC decisions, restrict the sample to the employees in firms with at least 20 employed
Focus on incumbent workers, i.e. those who do not leave or enter the respective firm during the sample period
Split into urban and rural subsamples by the firm's municipality (columns (2) and (3) of Tables 4-8)
sample.n_observations: 3,937,084 person-year observations in the full sample (2,626,844 urban; 1,310,240 rural), printed in Table 3 as 3937,084 / 2626,844 / 1310,240; 46,959 firm-year observations (29,525 urban; 17,434 rural)
sample.n_individuals: Not reported as a total; the text states about 250 thousand incumbent workers per year who do not switch their employer during 2001-2016

construction_notes: Outcome is the log-transformed annual growth rate in wage income; Table 3 reports mean 0.028 (SD 0.159) for the full sample, 0.029 (0.160) urban and 0.027 (0.157) rural, in units where 1 = 100 %
Offshoring dummy = 1 if one or more functions have been relocated internationally (inside the boundaries of the firm or via outsourcing) in period t
Backshoring dummy = 1 if the firm relocated activities from abroad to Denmark in period t; answer categories are only “Yes” or “No” and not by function
Survey waves have time gaps which were interpolated when constructing the treatment dummies: a firm that reported offshoring during 2001-2006 is assumed to continue until the next wave in 2009
Treatment dummies are measured at the firm level and vary unisono for all persons employed in the firm
Zm(i),t is the share of firms engaged in offshoring or backshoring at time t in the municipality i where the firm is located
Tenure in number of days employed enters in logs; firm size enters in logs
SME is defined as less than 250 employed in the firm following the EU definition in EU recommendation 2003/361

White-collar aggregates managerial, top-management and administrative occupations; blue-collar combines vocationally trained and semi-skilled occupations; unskilled & other occupations serve as the reference group
The reference group for the occupation dummies in Table 4 is employment without further information, which is distinct from “Occupation, others”

claims.statement: In the full sample pooling urban and rural firm locations, Offshore raises the annual wage growth of incumbent workers relative to incumbent workers in non-internationalizing firms (Table 4, column (1)).

register_source.value: Firm internationalization questionnaire data (VOUT, Danish International organization and outsourcing data), Statistics Denmark, matched to employed register data

definition.value: Binary dummy measured at the firm level, equal to 1 if firm m located in municipality i has offshored business activities in period t and 0 otherwise; the firm is taken to have offshored if one or more functions have been relocated internationally (inside the boundaries of the firm or via outsourcing). Coded from the retrospective VOUT survey question “Which activities has the firm outsourced in the period X to firms abroad?”, with waves covering 2001–2006, 2009–2011 and 2014–2016 and the gaps between waves interpolated.

timing.value: Measured at the firm level in the same year t as the wage-growth outcome; survey waves cover 2001–2006, 2009–2011 and 2014–2016 with the gaps interpolated

definition.value: ln(Δwage)k,m,t, the log-transformed annual growth rate in wage income of worker k employed in firm m located in i at time t; reported in Table 3 as “Wage growth rate (1 = 100 %)” with sample mean 0.028 and standard deviation 0.159. Wage growth rather than the wage level is used to capture dynamic effects.

timing.value: Annual, contemporaneous with the firm's offshoring/backshoring status in year t, over 2001–2016

units.value: change in the annual wage growth rate, in the units of Table 3 where 1 = 100 % (a coefficient of 0.003 is 0.3 percentage points of annual wage growth)

magnitude.interpretation: “a statistically significant increase in wage growth of 0.003, i.e., 0.3 %-points”

estimand.target_population: Incumbent workers employed throughout 2001–2016 in Danish private firms with at least 20 employees, urban and rural locations pooled that offshore business functions
estimand.time_horizon: Contemporaneous: annual wage growth in the same period t in which the firm is recorded as offshoring/backshoring; no lead or lag horizon is reported
estimand.formal_query: E[ln(Δwage)_do(offshore=1) − ln(Δwage)_do(offshore=0) | offshore=1] for incumbent workers in treated firms, urban and rural locations pooled

population.description: Incumbent workers in Danish private firms with at least 20 employees, urban and rural firm locations pooled, observed 2001–2016; incumbent workers are those who do not leave or enter the respective firm during the sample period
subgroups_defined: SME (fewer than 250 employed) vs larger firms
population.selection: Employees of private Danish firms with at least 20 employees covered by the VOUT firm survey, restricted to incumbent workers who remain with the same employer throughout the sample period

identification.source_of_variation: Within-worker changes over time in the employing firm's reported offshoring and backshoring status, from three Statistics Denmark VOUT firm surveys (2007, 2011, 2016, covering 2001–2006, 2009–2011 and 2014–2016), compared with incumbent workers in non-internationalizing firms, separately for urban and rural firm locations

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: absent the firm's offshoring/backshoring decision, wage growth of incumbent workers in GVC-reorganizing firms would have evolved like wage growth of incumbent workers in non-internationalizing firms, within urban and within rural locations.

Conditional on individual worker, industry (firm-specific sector) and time fixed effects and the observable worker, firm and municipality controls of Eq. (3), the firm's offshoring and backshoring decisions are unrelated to unobserved determinants of individual wage growth.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Multi-level fixed-effects structure (worker, industry, time) plus observable worker and firm characteristics; the paper states that identification relies on within-worker variation over time.

rhs: Unobserved determinants of individual wage growth
formal.as_written: ln(Δwage)k,m,t = α + δ⋅Xk,t + β⋅offshorem,t + θ⋅backshorem,t + π⋅Ym,t + λ⋅Zm(i),t + γk + γm(s) + γt + εk,m,t

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditioning the sample on incumbency — workers who neither leave nor enter the firm during 2001–2016 — does not bias the comparison; the paper argues it removes wage dynamics from job mobility rather than inducing selection.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued in the text as improving internal validity by reducing wage growth volatility due to job mobility among firms; no formal test.

implies_edges.from: Incumbency: worker stays with the same employer throughout 2001–2016

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the municipality-level share of firms offshoring and backshoring, the GVC decisions of other firms do not affect the wage growth of worker k in firm m (no residual spatial interference).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The share of firms engaged in offshoring or backshoring in the firm's municipality is included as control Zm(i),t.

implies_edges.from: Offshoring/backshoring by other firms in the municipality

key_assumptions.assumption: The interpolated treatment dummies (a firm reporting GVC activity in one survey wave is assumed to continue it until the next wave) measure the timing and duration of offshoring and backshoring well enough; the paper argues any resulting bias is downward.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued verbally as yielding conservative estimates; no sensitivity analysis reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: Offshoring and backshoring are treated as unrelated events, because backshoring cannot be matched to a specific previous offshoring event.
Firm-level survey answers on offshoring and backshoring apply to every workplace of the firm, so the corporate-level treatment can be assigned to the firm's urban or rural municipality.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors argue Danish municipalities are geographically large, that most firms are small or medium-sized, and that controlling for firm size alleviates the caveat; no test.

threats_discussed: Wage dynamics from job changes rather than the firm's GVC decision (addressed by restricting to incumbent workers)
Corporate-level survey answers cannot be assigned to individual workplaces within a corporate structure or family businesses with subsidiaries in several municipalities
Interpolation of treatment dummies across survey-wave gaps, argued to bias estimates downward

Voluntary participation of firms with 20–49 employees in manufacturing (NACE 15–37) and business services (NACE 72–74), which could reduce observed differences between offshoring and non-offshoring firms
Productivity and labour-demand spillovers from other offshoring/backshoring firms in the same municipality (controlled for by the municipality GVC shares)
unresolved_confounders: Offshoring and backshoring cannot be assigned at the corporate level to individual workplaces within a corporate structure or family businesses with several subsidiaries in different Danish municipalities
Backshoring cannot be linked to a specific previous offshoring event, so the two are treated as unrelated

definition.value: Linear combination of the offshore indicator, the occupation-group main effect and their interaction, reported in the lower part of Table 5; it gives the total wage-growth effect of offshore for workers in that occupation group relative to the unskilled & other reference group.

timing.value: Measured at the firm level in the same year t as the wage-growth outcome; survey waves cover 2001–2006, 2009–2011 and 2014–2016 with the gaps interpolated

definition.value: ln(Δwage)k,m,t, the log-transformed annual growth rate in wage income of worker k employed in firm m located in i at time t; reported in Table 3 as “Wage growth rate (1 = 100 %)” with sample mean 0.028 and standard deviation 0.159. Wage growth rather than the wage level is used to capture dynamic effects.

timing.value: Annual, contemporaneous with the firm's offshoring/backshoring status in year t, over 2001–2016

units.value: change in the annual wage growth rate, in the units of Table 3 where 1 = 100 % (a coefficient of 0.003 is 0.3 percentage points of annual wage growth)

estimand.target_population: Incumbent workers employed throughout 2001–2016 in Danish private firms with at least 20 employees, urban and rural locations pooled who are blue-collar workers in firms that offshore
estimand.time_horizon: Contemporaneous: annual wage growth in the same period t in which the firm is recorded as offshoring/backshoring; no lead or lag horizon is reported
estimand.formal_query: E[ln(Δwage)_do(offshore=1) − ln(Δwage)_do(offshore=0) | blue-collar workers, urban and rural locations pooled] (conditional average effect for blue-collar workers)

population.description: Incumbent workers in Danish private firms with at least 20 employees, urban and rural firm locations pooled, observed 2001–2016; incumbent workers are those who do not leave or enter the respective firm during the sample period
subgroups_defined: SME (fewer than 250 employed) vs larger firms
population.selection: Employees of private Danish firms with at least 20 employees covered by the VOUT firm survey, restricted to incumbent workers who remain with the same employer throughout the sample period

identification.source_of_variation: Within-worker changes over time in the employing firm's reported offshoring and backshoring status, from three Statistics Denmark VOUT firm surveys (2007, 2011, 2016, covering 2001–2006, 2009–2011 and 2014–2016), compared with incumbent workers in non-internationalizing firms, separately for urban and rural firm locations

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: absent the firm's offshoring/backshoring decision, wage growth of incumbent workers in GVC-reorganizing firms would have evolved like wage growth of incumbent workers in non-internationalizing firms, within urban and within rural locations.

Conditional on individual worker, industry (firm-specific sector) and time fixed effects and the observable worker, firm and municipality controls of Eq. (3), the firm's offshoring and backshoring decisions are unrelated to unobserved determinants of individual wage growth.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Multi-level fixed-effects structure (worker, industry, time) plus observable worker and firm characteristics; the paper states that identification relies on within-worker variation over time.

rhs: Unobserved determinants of individual wage growth
formal.as_written: ln(Δwage)k,m,t = α + δ⋅Xk,t + β⋅offshorem,t + θ⋅backshorem,t + π⋅Ym,t + λ⋅Zm(i),t + γk + γm(s) + γt + εk,m,t

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditioning the sample on incumbency — workers who neither leave nor enter the firm during 2001–2016 — does not bias the comparison; the paper argues it removes wage dynamics from job mobility rather than inducing selection.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued in the text as improving internal validity by reducing wage growth volatility due to job mobility among firms; no formal test.

implies_edges.from: Incumbency: worker stays with the same employer throughout 2001–2016

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the municipality-level share of firms offshoring and backshoring, the GVC decisions of other firms do not affect the wage growth of worker k in firm m (no residual spatial interference).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The share of firms engaged in offshoring or backshoring in the firm's municipality is included as control Zm(i),t.

implies_edges.from: Offshoring/backshoring by other firms in the municipality

key_assumptions.assumption: The interpolated treatment dummies (a firm reporting GVC activity in one survey wave is assumed to continue it until the next wave) measure the timing and duration of offshoring and backshoring well enough; the paper argues any resulting bias is downward.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued verbally as yielding conservative estimates; no sensitivity analysis reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: Offshoring and backshoring are treated as unrelated events, because backshoring cannot be matched to a specific previous offshoring event.
Firm-level survey answers on offshoring and backshoring apply to every workplace of the firm, so the corporate-level treatment can be assigned to the firm's urban or rural municipality.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors argue Danish municipalities are geographically large, that most firms are small or medium-sized, and that controlling for firm size alleviates the caveat; no test.

threats_discussed: Wage dynamics from job changes rather than the firm's GVC decision (addressed by restricting to incumbent workers)
Corporate-level survey answers cannot be assigned to individual workplaces within a corporate structure or family businesses with subsidiaries in several municipalities
Interpolation of treatment dummies across survey-wave gaps, argued to bias estimates downward

Voluntary participation of firms with 20–49 employees in manufacturing (NACE 15–37) and business services (NACE 72–74), which could reduce observed differences between offshoring and non-offshoring firms
Productivity and labour-demand spillovers from other offshoring/backshoring firms in the same municipality (controlled for by the municipality GVC shares)
unresolved_confounders: Offshoring and backshoring cannot be assigned at the corporate level to individual workplaces within a corporate structure or family businesses with several subsidiaries in different Danish municipalities
Backshoring cannot be linked to a specific previous offshoring event, so the two are treated as unrelated

definition.value: Binary dummy measured at the firm level, equal to 1 if firm m located in municipality i has offshored business activities in period t and 0 otherwise; the firm is taken to have offshored if one or more functions have been relocated internationally (inside the boundaries of the firm or via outsourcing). key_assumptions.assumption: Conditioning the sample on incumbency — workers who neither leave nor enter the firm during 2001–2016 — does not bias the comparison; the paper argues it removes wage dynamics from job mobility rather than inducing selection.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued in the text as improving internal validity by reducing wage growth volatility due to job mobility among firms; no formal test.

implies_edges.from: Incumbency: worker stays with the same employer throughout 2001–2016

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the municipality-level share of firms offshoring and backshoring, the GVC decisions of other firms do not affect the wage growth of worker k in firm m (no residual spatial interference).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The share of firms engaged in offshoring or backshoring in the firm's municipality is included as control Zm(i),t.

implies_edges.from: Offshoring/backshoring by other firms in the municipality

key_assumptions.assumption: The interpolated treatment dummies (a firm reporting GVC activity in one survey wave is assumed to continue it until the next wave) measure the timing and duration of offshoring and backshoring well enough; the paper argues any resulting bias is downward.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued verbally as yielding conservative estimates; no sensitivity analysis reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: Offshoring and backshoring are treated as unrelated events, because backshoring cannot be matched to a specific previous offshoring event.
Firm-level survey answers on offshoring and backshoring apply to every workplace of the firm, so the corporate-level treatment can be assigned to the firm's urban or rural municipality.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors argue Danish municipalities are geographically large, that most firms are small or medium-sized, and that controlling for firm size alleviates the caveat; no test.

threats_discussed: Wage dynamics from job changes rather than the firm's GVC decision (addressed by restricting to incumbent workers)
Corporate-level survey answers cannot be assigned to individual workplaces within a corporate structure or family businesses with subsidiaries in several municipalities
Interpolation of treatment dummies across survey-wave gaps, argued to bias estimates downward

Voluntary participation of firms with 20–49 employees in manufacturing (NACE 15–37) and business services (NACE 72–74), which could reduce observed differences between offshoring and non-offshoring firms
Productivity and labour-demand spillovers from other offshoring/backshoring firms in the same municipality (controlled for by the municipality GVC shares)
unresolved_confounders: Offshoring and backshoring cannot be assigned at the corporate level to individual workplaces within a corporate structure or family businesses with several subsidiaries in different Danish municipalities
Backshoring cannot be linked to a specific previous offshoring event, so the two are treated as unrelated

ambiguities: Parentheses in Table 8 hold t statistics, not standard errors or confidence intervals; se_or_ci transcribes the printed t statistic and se/ci_low/ci_high are left null.
baseline_mean is the sample mean of wage growth for the corresponding column of Table 3 (full/urban/rural); the paper prints no separate control-group mean.
Table 8's note says the number of observations is reduced because detailed offshoring/backshoring information is missing in some instances, yet the printed N equals that of Tables 4–7.

evidence.how: Eq. (3) regresses ln(Δwage)k,m,t on offshorem,t and backshorem,t dated in the same period t, so the estimated horizon is contemporaneous (0 years); the paper states no lead or lag horizon.
Statistical significance read off the printed stars against the table note legend (* p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001); 1 star(s) printed on this coefficient.
